Analysis of deviance for fixed effects

Source: R/ilm_anova.R, R/zzz-iml-aliases.R
ilm_anova.Rd

Tests each fixed-effect term jointly: all of its coefficients at once, and for a multinomial outcome across all category dimensions.

Usage

ilm_anova(
  object,
  type = 2,
  test = c("Wald", "LRT"),
  ncores = 1L,
  restarts = 2L,
  recode = TRUE,
  df = "auto",
  statistic = c("F", "Chisq")
)

Arguments

object

A fitted "ilm_model" object, fitted through the formula interface.

type

2 or "II" (the default), or 3 or "III". Type II tests each term against everything not containing it, which does not depend on how the factors are coded. Type III tests each term against every other, which does – see recode.

test

"Wald" or "LRT". A likelihood-ratio test compares maximum-likelihood fits, so a REML fit is refitted by maximum likelihood for it, with a message; the fit passed in is unchanged. For a gaussian mixed or dispersion model the Wald F test needs no refit (see the section on unequal spreads).

ncores

Integer. Worker processes for the refits.

restarts

Integer. Optimiser restarts in refits.

recode

When type = 3 and a term inside an interaction is coded in a way that makes its main-effect row something other than a Type III test, refit with stats::contr.sum() for those factors and say so. FALSE tests the model exactly as coded and warns instead. The fit passed in is never modified either way.

df

For the Wald tests of a gaussian mixed model, or of a gaussian model with a dispersion formula and no random terms, the denominator degrees of freedom of each F: "auto" (Satterthwaite's, as lmerTest reports), "satterthwaite", "kenward-roger" (their df and scaled F, on their adjusted covariance; REML fits) or "asymptotic". Other fits are unaffected. For a term of several columns, Satterthwaite's df combines the columns' own df by Fai and Cornelius (1996), which is defined only when each has more than 2 df; otherwise the term's DenDF and p-value are NA and the table's heading says why. Kenward-Roger's df, or testing fewer contrasts at once, may give one.

statistic

"F" (the default) or "Chisq". For the Wald tests of a gaussian mixed model, or of a gaussian dispersion model with no random terms, "F" gives an F test on the denominator df above and "Chisq" the large-sample chi-square the table gave before; with few groups the chi-square is too liberal. Every other fit keeps its own reference: exact F with nothing integrated out, chi-square otherwise.

Value

An "anova" data frame with one row per fixed-effect term. The columns are Df, Chisq and Pr(>Chisq) in general; Df, F value and Pr(>F) when the model admits exact inference – a gaussian model with no random or smooth terms, where the residual variance is estimated rather than assumed known (see ilm_model()); and NumDF, DenDF, F value and Pr(>F) for the Wald tests of a gaussian mixed model, or of a gaussian dispersion model with no random terms, with statistic = "F". A model with no terms to test, such as an intercept-only model, returns a table with zero rows rather than an error: "there is nothing to test" is an answer, not a failure.

Why this exists rather than car

:Anova: car::Anova() reads the assign attribute of the model matrix, which has one entry per design column. A multinomial fit has C coefficients per column, so car would match a short vector against a long one and silently test only the first category, reporting df = 1 where the correct joint test has df = C. It returns a plausible table that answers the wrong question. illume registers its own method so that car::Anova() dispatches here and gets the right answer.

Type II versus Type III

Type III tests each term with every other term in the model. Type II tests each term after all terms that do not contain it, respecting marginality. They agree when there are no interactions.

With interactions present, Type II is usually preferred for main effects, and it has the practical advantage of not depending on how factors are coded. Type III does depend on the coding and is only well defined with orthogonal contrasts such as stats::contr.sum().

Unequal spreads, and Welch's test

A gaussian model with a spread per group, dispformula = ~ group, and no random terms gets F tests on Satterthwaite's denominator df by default, combined over a term's columns by Fai and Cornelius (1996). Fitted by REML, which is that model's default, the F test of the group term has Welch's (1951) numerator exactly. With two groups it is Welch's t test: the same statistic, df and p-value as t.test(var.equal = FALSE). With three or more, Welch divides the statistic by \(1 + 2(k - 2)\Lambda/(k^2 - 1)\) and uses \((k^2 - 1)/(3\Lambda)\) denominator df, where \(\Lambda = \sum_i (1 - w_i/W)^2/(n_i - 1)\), \(w_i = n_i/s_i^2\) and \(W = \sum_i w_i\); the df here come instead from Satterthwaite's approximation, which applies to any design, not only one factor. So with three or more groups the F here is somewhat larger than Welch's and its df differ, and stats::oneway.test() gives Welch's own.

In a simulation over 14 designs, under equal means at a nominal 5%, this F rejected a median 5.8% of the time (4% to 10%), against Welch's 5.1% in the one-way designs. With normal errors, Welch held 5% better with four or six groups of six to eight observations (6.1% against 6.7%, and 5.2% against 6.6%); a one-degree-of-freedom term beside other terms, and a spread modelled on a covariate in 20 observations, came out near 7% to 8%. Fitted by maximum likelihood the F is larger again, because the group variances are divided by \(n_i\) rather than \(n_i - 1\), and too liberal: a median 8.2%, up to 14.5%. statistic = "Chisq" gives the large-sample chi-square, which rejected a median 11.5% on a maximum-likelihood fit, up to 26%.

Wald versus likelihood ratio

Wald tests are fast and need no refitting for Type III. Likelihood-ratio tests refit a reduced model for each term, which is slower but avoids the Hauck-Donner effect, where a Wald statistic can shrink for very strong effects. If a term is important to your conclusions, confirm it with the LRT; for small samples use ilm_pb_lrt() instead, since both rely on large-sample approximations.

References

Fox, J., & Weisberg, S. (2019). An R Companion to Applied Regression, 3rd ed. Sage. (Chapter 5 explains Type II and Type III tests.)

Fai, A. H.-T., & Cornelius, P. L. (1996). Approximate F-tests of multiple degree of freedom hypotheses in generalized least squares analyses of unbalanced split-plot experiments. Journal of Statistical Computation and Simulation, 54(4), 363–378.

Hauck, W. W., & Donner, A. (1977). Wald's test as applied to hypotheses in logit analysis. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 72(360), 851–853.

Satterthwaite, F. E. (1946). An approximate distribution of estimates of variance components. Biometrics Bulletin, 2(6), 110–114.

Welch, B. L. (1951). On the comparison of several mean values: An alternative approach. Biometrika, 38(3/4), 330–336.
